title: How do you create an immutable class in Java (final class, private final fields, no setters, defensive copies)?
shortTitle: How do you create an immutable class in Java?

s1_definition.profdef: An immutable class is one whose instances cannot change state after construction. You create one by making the class `final` so it cannot be subclassed and weakened, making all fields `private` and `final` so they are set exactly once in the constructor, providing no setters or any mutating methods, and making defensive copies of any mutable objects both when they are passed into the constructor and when they are returned from getters. Any operation that would conceptually change the object instead returns a new instance. This guarantees the object's observable state is fixed for its entire lifetime.
s1_definition.analogy: At the National Bank of India, an immutable object is like a printed and stamped demand draft. Once the draft for a fixed amount is issued to Rajesh, nobody can alter the amount, the date, or the payee on that piece of paper. If Rajesh needs a different amount, the bank does not edit the old draft; it cancels nothing and simply issues a brand-new draft. The original stays exactly as printed forever. That is what immutability means: the object is fixed at creation, and any change produces a new object instead of modifying the old one.
s1_definition.oneliner: Make the class final, fields private final, no setters, defensively copy mutable inputs and outputs, and return new instances for any change.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** An immutable class is one whose instances cannot change state after construction. You create one by making the class `final` so it cannot be subclassed and weakened, making all fields `private` and `final` so they are set exactly once in the constructor, providing no setters or any mutating methods, and making defensive copies of any mutable objects both when they are passed into the constructor and when they are returned from getters. Any operation that would conceptually change the object instead returns a new instance. This guarantees the object's observable state is fixed for its entire lifetime.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** At the National Bank of India, an immutable object is like a printed and stamped demand draft. Once the draft for a fixed amount is issued to Rajesh, nobody can alter the amount, the date, or the payee on that piece of paper. If Rajesh needs a different amount, the bank does not edit the old draft; it cancels nothing and simply issues a brand-new draft. The original stays exactly as printed forever. That is what immutability means: the object is fixed at creation, and any change produces a new object instead of modifying the old one.

**One line to remember:** Make the class final, fields private final, no setters, defensively copy mutable inputs and outputs, and return new instances for any change.

sections.s2_technical:
The first rule is to make the class `final`. If the class can be subclassed, a subclass could add mutable state or override methods to break the immutability contract, so sealing the class protects the guarantee. An alternative to final is to make all constructors private and provide static factories, but final is the simplest.

The second rule is that every field is `private` and `final`. Private prevents outside code from touching the field, and final ensures the field is assigned exactly once, in the constructor, and never reassigned. This also gives a thread-safety guarantee from the Java Memory Model: once the constructor completes, all threads see the correctly initialized final fields without synchronization.

The third rule is no setters and no mutating methods. There must be no method that changes any field. Operations that conceptually modify the value, such as adding money, return a brand-new instance with the new value rather than changing the current one.

The fourth and most subtle rule is defensive copying for mutable fields. If a field is itself a mutable type, like a `Date`, a `List`, or an array, then simply storing the reference is not enough, because the caller could keep their own reference and mutate the object after construction. So you copy the mutable object in the constructor, and you also copy it again when returning it from a getter, so no external code ever gets a reference to your internal mutable state. For collections you can wrap in an unmodifiable view, but a true defensive copy is safer because an unmodifiable view over a list you still share can be bypassed if the original is mutated.

A senior nuance is that immutable objects are inherently thread-safe and freely shareable with no synchronization, because there is no mutable state to race on. This is why `String`, the wrapper classes, `BigDecimal`, and Java records are immutable. Records, introduced in Java 16, give you a concise immutable data carrier, though you still need defensive copies inside a compact constructor if a component is mutable. Another nuance is that immutability enables safe caching and use as map keys, because the hash code never changes.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank represents money and a transaction record that must never change once created, because an audit trail depends on records being tamper-proof. This is exactly what an immutable class guarantees.

Problem 2 — A transaction record holds a list of line items. If the bank stored the caller's list directly, the caller could add items later and silently alter the record. This is exactly why defensive copying of the mutable list is required, both in and out.

Problem 3 — When money needs to be added, the bank must produce a new Money object rather than editing the old one. This is exactly the return-a-new-instance pattern.

The code has an immutable `Money` class, an immutable `TransactionRecord` with a defensively copied list, and an `ImmutableClassDemo` main class that proves the record cannot be changed from outside.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: a Money of 50000, an add of 10000, and a transaction record TXN-001 with a list containing one line item.

Step 1: Money m1 is created with 50000. Its amount field is private and final, so it is fixed at construction.

Step 2: m1.add produces m2 with 60000. Crucially, m1 is not changed; a brand-new Money instance is returned. This proves the return-a-new-instance pattern.

Step 3: A TransactionRecord TXN-001 is created with the caller's list. Inside the constructor, the list is defensively copied into a new ArrayList, so the record holds its own private copy.

Step 4: The caller then adds "FAKE ENTRY" to its original list. Because the record copied the list, the record's items are unaffected, still containing only the original entry. The defensive copy on the way in protected the record.

Step 5: The caller tries to tamper through the getter by adding to the returned list. Because the getter returns an unmodifiable view, the add throws UnsupportedOperationException, which is caught and logged. The defensive output protection blocked the tamper.

Step 6: The final record is logged, showing it remained exactly as constructed. The object's observable state never changed after construction, which is the definition of immutability.

```text
INFO: m1 (unchanged) = Rs.50000, m2 (new) = Rs.60000
INFO: Caller mutated its list; record items still = [TRANSFER SAV2001->CUR3001]
INFO: Returned list is unmodifiable; tamper blocked
INFO: Final record = TXN-001 Rs.50000 items=[TRANSFER SAV2001->CUR3001]
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```text
  new Money(50000)  → m1.amount = 50000 (private final, fixed)
    │ add(10000)
    ▼ returns NEW instance
  m2.amount = 60000     (m1 STILL 50000 — unchanged)

  new TransactionRecord("TXN-001", 50000, callerList)
    │ constructor: this.items = new ArrayList<>(callerList)  ← defensive copy IN
    ▼
  callerList.add("FAKE")  → record.items UNAFFECTED
    │
    ▼ getItems()
  returns Collections.unmodifiableList(items)  ← defensive OUT
    │ .add("ANOTHER FAKE")
    ▼
  UnsupportedOperationException  (tamper blocked)
```

sections.s5d_lld:
```text
  ═══ LLD — Immutable Class Recipe ═══

  ┌───────────────────────────────────────┐
  │   <<final>> TransactionRecord         │
  │ ─────────────────────────────────────│
  │ - final id: String                    │  private final
  │ - final amount: Money (immutable)     │  private final
  │ - final items: List<String>           │  private final (copied)
  │ ─────────────────────────────────────│
  │ ctor: items = new ArrayList<>(in)     │  ← defensive copy IN
  │ + getItems(): unmodifiableList(items) │  ← defensive copy OUT
  │ (NO setters, NO mutators)             │
  └───────────────────────────────────────┘

  The 5-rule recipe:
   1 final class            (no subclass weakening)
   2 private final fields   (assign once)
   3 no setters/mutators    (operations return NEW instance)
   4 defensive copy IN+OUT  (for mutable fields: List/Date/array)
   5 (optional) static factory instead of final if subclassing needed

  Thread-safety: inherently safe — no mutable state to race on.
  Modern option: record TransactionRecord(...) + compact ctor copy.
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
An immutable class is one whose instances cannot change state after construction, and I build one by following a clear recipe. First, I make the class final so no subclass can extend it and weaken the guarantee. Second, I make every field private and final, so each field is assigned exactly once in the constructor and never reassigned. Third, I provide no setters and no mutating methods; any operation that conceptually changes the value, like adding money, returns a brand-new instance instead of modifying the current one. Fourth, and most subtly, I make defensive copies of any mutable fields, both when they come into the constructor and when they go out through a getter, so that no external code ever holds a reference to my internal mutable state.

That fourth rule is where most people slip. If my record holds a list, and I store the caller's list directly, the caller can keep their reference and add items later, silently corrupting my object. So in the constructor I copy the incoming list into a new list, and in the getter I return an unmodifiable view or a fresh copy, which blocks tampering from both directions.

The reason immutability matters so much, especially in banking, is that immutable objects are inherently thread-safe and freely shareable with no synchronization at all, because there is simply no mutable state to race on. This is exactly why String, the wrapper classes, and BigDecimal are immutable, and it is also the guarantee behind Java records, which give me a concise immutable data carrier, though I still add defensive copies in a compact constructor if a component is mutable. Immutability also makes an object safe to cache and to use as a map key, because its hash code never changes.

In our ledger service, audit records are immutable for precisely this reason. Once a transaction record is created, it is tamper-proof, and I can share it across the audit service, the reporting service, and caches at the same time without a single lock, which is both safer and faster than guarding mutable records with synchronization.

---

keyPoints: Declare the class final — prevent subclassing
Defensive copy mutable fields in constructor and getters
Example: String, Integer, LocalDate are all immutable
